title: The sign of the cross, again
hookLine: the smallest prayer you learned on day two
tomorrow: Mia's coming to Mass on Sunday. what will she see?

cards: Penalty kick. Before the run-up, the player touches forehead, chest, one shoulder, then the other, in about a second. The cameras catch it; nobody comments.
It's the smallest prayer there is, and one of the first this path taught: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. So, years later, a question with two good answers.
Is it better quick and often, or slow and rare?

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER.
teach.b: The words come from the end of Matthew, where Jesus sends his friends out baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." The gesture has two Catholic voices pulling different ways.
First, Tertullian, an early Christian writer from North Africa.
He describes Christians tracing the sign on their foreheads at every turn: going in and out, putting on shoes, bathing, sitting down to eat, lighting the lamps.
His case: make it often, and the whole ordinary day gets marked as God's, not only the big moments. A quick cross before a penalty kick fits him fine.
Then the theologian Romano Guardini, who asks for the opposite: not a hurried, cramped flick, but a large, slow sign, forehead to breast, shoulder to shoulder, felt all the way.
His case: made slowly, it gathers the whole person, thoughts, heart and body, under the cross, and it stays a prayer instead of becoming a twitch.
One to tell a friend: in Tertullian's description, the sign is traced on the forehead, not drawn large from shoulder to shoulder.
Both voices are Catholic. And both agree on the thing that matters: it's a prayer, a name spoken over a body.

how: Catholics make the sign of the cross at the start and end of prayers and of Mass, with holy water entering a church, and before meals, games, journeys or hard moments; some trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart before the Gospel.

games.q: what does “the sign of the cross” mean?
o: a prayer traced over the body in the Trinity's name
a good-luck gesture athletes make before a game
a salute Catholics give when passing a church

games.q: two ways to make it — tap the pairs.
p: in the name of the Father, Son, Holy Ghost
on the forehead, at every turn
large and slow, felt all the way
it's a prayer, not a twitch

s: Tertullian describes a big cross drawn from shoulder to shoulder
he describes tracing it on the forehead, at every turn of the day.
the words of the sign come from Jesus sending his friends to baptize
in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Matthew 28.
the Church has one official speed for the sign of the cross
Tertullian made it often; Guardini urged slow and large. both are Catholic voices.

games.q: you make the sign slowly, Guardini-style. your teammate crosses herself fast, a dozen times a game, and says Tertullian's on her side. what's her best case?
o: quick signs at every turn mark the whole day as God's, not only big moments.
speed doesn't matter because the sign is only a habit, not a prayer.
slow signs are showing off; prayer should always stay hidden.
games.why: Tertullian's Christians traced it going in and out, dressing, eating, lighting lamps. Guardini's answer: then let each one, however quick, still be a prayer.

practice: Make the sign of the cross the slow way: hand to forehead, Father; down to the heart, Son; shoulder to shoulder, Holy Ghost. Give each touch a few seconds, and feel where your hand lands.
If you don't pray, simply notice the shape the gesture draws over you.

wordCard.voice: The sign of the cross. A name traced over the body: quick at every turn, or slow and large, and a prayer either way.

orig.note: Greek: cross. the New Testament's word for the cross of Jesus.

carryVoice: Your line: where it began, a hand on the forehead and a name. Until tomorrow.
